title: Tutankhamun's Tomb: The Last Season, the First Step and the 'Curse'
description: By 1922 Howard Carter had searched the Valley of the Kings for years and his sponsor was ready to quit. He was given one final season. Three days in, a single stone step appeared in the sand. This is the story of how the tomb of Tutankhamun was found, what was inside, and how the legend of a curse began.

sources.title: Discovery of the tomb of Tutankhamun, Wikipedia

Howard Carter and the Discovery of King Tut's Tomb, HistoryNet

lines.t: Jack, how long would you keep digging in a desert valley if you found almost nothing?
A season? Maybe two.
Howard Carter kept going for years. And by 1922, the man paying for it had had enough.
So he was told to stop.
He was given one last season. Three days after work began, one of his crew uncovered a step cut into the rock.
One step.
One step. Behind it was the most complete royal burial ever found in Egypt. And a story about a curse that newspapers still love.

chapters.heading: The Valley Everyone Thought Was Empty
image_queries: Valley of the Kings tombs entrance

lines.t: The Valley of the Kings, near Luxor, is where Egypt's New Kingdom pharaohs were buried. Dozens of tombs are cut into its cliffs.
And all of them had been robbed.
Nearly all, and long ago. By the early 1900s, one wealthy excavator declared the valley exhausted.
Carter did not agree.
Carter was an English artist who became an archaeologist. He had noticed small finds bearing the name of a little-known king: Tutankhamun. Embalming materials, a cup, bits of gold foil.
Clues that a tomb was nearby.
That was his hunch. His sponsor was George Herbert, the Earl of Carnarvon, a rich amateur whose home was Highclere Castle in England.
They worked the valley for season after season, clearing it down to bedrock, section by section.
By the summer of 1922 Carnarvon wanted to stop. The cost was high and the results were thin.
How did Carter change his mind?
He pleaded for one more season to finish a single remaining patch, near the entrance to the tomb of Ramesses the Sixth. Carnarvon agreed.
Digging began on the 1st of November. The crew cleared the remains of ancient workmen's huts.
And on the fourth?
On the 4th of November 1922, a step appeared beneath the huts. Tradition says a water boy found it. By the next day they had cleared a staircase leading down to a sealed doorway.
Did Carter open it?
No. He had the stairs filled back in and sent a telegram to England: "At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley; a magnificent tomb with seals intact."
And then he waited.
For almost three weeks, until Carnarvon arrived.
When the doorway was fully cleared, they saw seals with the name Tutankhamun. They also saw that the door had been broken and resealed in ancient times.
So robbers had been inside.
At least twice, soon after the burial. But they had not taken much.
On the 26th of November, Carter made a small hole in a second door and held up a candle.
This is the famous line.
Carnarvon asked if he could see anything. In Carter's published account, he answered: "Yes, wonderful things."
What was he looking at?
A room packed to the ceiling. Gilded couches shaped like animals, dismantled chariots, chests, statues, food boxes, a golden throne.
More than five thousand objects were eventually recorded. Carter's team photographed, drew and numbered each one before moving it. Clearing the tomb took about ten years.
Who was Tutankhamun, actually?
A minor king. He came to the throne as a child, around 1332 BC, and died about nine years later, at eighteen or nineteen.
So not a great conqueror.
Not at all. His reign mattered mostly because it reversed the religious revolution of Akhenaten, who was very probably his father.
Then why such a rich tomb?
That is the point. It is actually a small tomb, likely not built for a king. If this is what a minor pharaoh received, imagine what the great ones had before the robbers came.
The burial chamber was officially opened in February 1923. Inside were four gilded shrines, one inside another, then a stone sarcophagus, then three coffins.
Like nesting dolls.
The innermost coffin is solid gold and weighs about a hundred and ten kilograms. On the mummy's face lay the gold mask, about ten kilograms on its own.
In April 1923, a few months after the opening, Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo.
Here comes the curse.
He had been bitten by a mosquito, cut the bite while shaving, and developed blood poisoning. He was already in poor health.
But the newspapers had a better explanation.
Much better. Stories spread of a curse on anyone who disturbed the king. No such curse inscription was found in the tomb.
Did the others die too?
Later studies compared the people present at the opening with those who were not. There was no real difference in how long they lived.
Carter himself, who spent a decade inside the tomb, died in 1939, at sixty-four.
Where did the treasure go?
Unlike many earlier finds, it stayed in Egypt. Egypt had just become formally independent, and the government insisted the collection remain together.
That caused arguments, I imagine.
Serious ones. At one point Carter was locked out of the tomb. But the principle held.
For decades the objects were in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. Now the collection is displayed together at the Grand Egyptian Museum near the pyramids of Giza.
And the king?
His mummy still rests in the tomb in the valley.
The part I cannot get over is the timing. Three days into the final season.
And under huts that earlier excavators had left alone. The tomb survived because it was forgotten.
A forgotten king, famous because nobody remembered him.
Would you have kept digging for that long?
Tell us in the comments.
